nodes.text: We call $m$ practical if every integer $1\leq n<m$ is the sum of distinct divisors of $m$. If $m$ is practical then let $h(m)$ be such that $h(m)$ many divisors always suffice. Are there infinitely many practical $m$ such that\[h(m) < (\log\log m)^{O(1)}?\]Is it true that $h(n!)<n^{o(1)}$? Or perhaps even $h(n!)<(\log n)^{O(1)}$?

#18 : [Er74b] [Er79] [ErGr80] [Er81h,p.172] [Er95] [Er96b] [Er98] number theory | divisors | factorials It is easy to see that almost all numbers are not practical. Erdős originally showed that $h(n!) <n$. Vose [Vo85] proved the existence of infinitely many practical $m$ such that $h(m)\ll (\log m)^{1/2}$. The sequence of practical numbers is A005153 in the OEIS. The reward of \$250 is offered in [Er81h] for a proof or disproof of whether\[h(n) <(\log \log n)^{O(1)}\]for infinitely many practical $n$. See also [304] and [825] .
